Interpreting local LLM Throughput Measurements: A Technical Guide

When evaluating the performance of a locally deployed large language model (LLM), throughput is one of the most critical metrics to understand. Throughput, in this context, refers to the number of tokens or prompts that can be processed per unit of time — typically measured in tokens per second (t/s) or prompts per second (p/s). However, interpreting these numbers correctly requires a nuanced understanding of how they are measured, what factors influence them, and how they should be contextualized. This technical note will walk through the key components of throughput measurement, including prompt throughput, generation throughput, batch effects, context length effects, warm cache effects, the misleading nature of very short outputs, and how to compare CPU-only, GPU-only, and hybrid runs.

Prompt Throughput vs. Generation Throughput

It is essential to distinguish between prompt throughput and generation throughput. Prompt throughput refers to the rate at which the model can process input prompts — that is, the time it takes to decode the prompt and prepare for generation. Generation throughput, on the other hand, refers to the rate at which the model generates output tokens after the prompt has been processed. In many benchmarks, especially those that measure “throughput,” the metric is often reported as generation throughput — the number of tokens generated per second — because it is more directly related to the model’s utility in real-world applications.

However, prompt throughput is equally important, especially in scenarios where the model is used to process many short prompts in parallel. For example, in a chatbot system, the prompt throughput determines how quickly the model can respond to incoming user messages. If the prompt processing is slow, even if the generation is fast, the overall system latency will be high. Therefore, when interpreting throughput measurements, it is crucial to know whether the metric includes prompt processing or not.

Batch Effects

Batching is a technique used to improve throughput by processing multiple prompts simultaneously. When a model is run in batch mode, the hardware (CPU or GPU) can perform operations in parallel, which can significantly increase throughput. However, batching also introduces overhead — the model must manage multiple input sequences, which can increase memory usage and computational load. The effect of batching is not linear: as batch size increases, throughput may increase, but only up to a point. Beyond that, the overhead of managing larger batches can cause throughput to plateau or even decrease.

For example, if you run a model with a batch size of 1, you might get 100 tokens per second. With a batch size of 4, you might get 350 tokens per second — a 3.5x improvement. But with a batch size of 16, you might only get 500 tokens per second — a 1.4x improvement over the batch size 4 run. This is because the model’s attention mechanism and memory management become more complex with larger batches, and the hardware may not be able to fully parallelize the operations.

Context Length Effects

Context length — the maximum number of tokens the model can process in a single forward pass — has a significant impact on throughput. Longer context lengths require more memory and computational resources, which can slow down the model. For example, a model that can handle 4096 tokens may process a 1024-token prompt at 200 tokens per second, but when processing a 4096-token prompt, the throughput may drop to 50 tokens per second.

This is because the model must maintain more internal states and compute more attention weights. Additionally, longer context lengths may require more memory bandwidth, which can become a bottleneck on certain hardware. Therefore, when interpreting throughput measurements, it is important to know the context length used. A model that achieves 1000 tokens per second on a 1024-token prompt may only achieve 200 tokens per second on a 4096-token prompt — a 5x slowdown.

Warm Cache Effects

The “warm cache” effect refers to the performance improvement that occurs when the model’s cache is preloaded with frequently used data. In the context of LLMs, this means that if the model has previously processed similar prompts or sequences, it can reuse cached computations, which can significantly improve throughput. For example, if you run a model multiple times with the same prompt, the first run may be slow because the model must compute everything from scratch. However, subsequent runs may be faster because the model can reuse cached computations.

This effect is particularly important in applications where the same prompts are repeated frequently — such as in chatbots or recommendation systems. However, it is also important to note that the warm cache effect is not always present. If the prompts are very different, or if the model is run on different hardware, the cache may not be effective. Therefore, when interpreting throughput measurements, it is important to know whether the model was run with a warm cache or not.

Why Very Short Outputs Are Misleading

One of the most common pitfalls in interpreting LLM throughput is the use of very short outputs — for example, a single token or a few tokens. These outputs are often used to measure “throughput” because they are easy to compute and because they can be generated quickly. However, they are misleading because they do not reflect the model’s true performance.

For example, if you measure the throughput of a model that generates a single token, you may get a very high number — perhaps 1000 tokens per second. However, if you measure the throughput of the same model generating a 100-token output, you may get a much lower number — perhaps 100 tokens per second. This is because the model must compute more attention weights and more internal states for longer outputs, which can slow down the model.

Therefore, when interpreting throughput measurements, it is important to use outputs that are representative of the model’s intended use. For example, if the model is intended to generate long-form text, then the throughput should be measured using long outputs. If the model is intended to generate short-form text, then the throughput should be measured using short outputs.

Comparing CPU-Only, GPU-Only, and Hybrid Runs

Finally, it is important to understand how to compare throughput measurements across different hardware configurations — CPU-only, GPU-only, and hybrid runs. Each configuration has its own strengths and weaknesses, and the throughput will vary accordingly.

CPU-only runs are typically slower than GPU-only runs because CPUs are not optimized for parallel computation. However, they are more accessible and can be used on systems that do not have GPUs. GPU-only runs are typically faster because GPUs are optimized for parallel computation. However, they require more memory and may be more expensive.

Hybrid runs — which use both CPU and GPU — can offer the best of both worlds. For example, the CPU can handle the prompt processing, while the GPU handles the generation. This can improve throughput and reduce latency. However, hybrid runs also introduce overhead — the model must manage data transfer between the CPU and GPU, which can slow down the model.

Therefore, when comparing throughput measurements across different hardware configurations, it is important to know the specific use case. For example, if the model is intended to be used on a system with limited GPU resources, then the CPU-only throughput may be more relevant. If the model is intended to be used on a system with high GPU resources, then the GPU-only throughput may be more relevant.
